what_its_for: Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including breast cancer, ovarian cancer, lung cancer, and Kaposi's sarcoma. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing, which helps slow or stop the spread of cancer in your body.
how_to_take: Paclitaxel is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor at a hospital or cancer treatment center. You will NOT take this medicine at home as a pill or injection. Each infusion session can take anywhere from 1 to 24 hours depending on your treatment plan. Before your infusion, you will usually be given other medicines (such as steroids and antihistamines) to help prevent allergic reactions. Make sure to drink plenty of fluids before and after your treatment unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
dosing: Your dose of paclitaxel is carefully calculated by your cancer care team based on your body size (height and weight), the type of cancer being treated, and your overall health. A common schedule is receiving the infusion once every 3 weeks, once a week, or according to a special plan your doctor designs for you. Never try to change your dose or schedule on your own. Always follow exactly what your oncology team tells you.
missed_dose: Since paclitaxel is given to you by healthcare professionals at a clinic or hospital, it is unlikely you will miss a dose on your own. However, if you need to cancel or reschedule your appointment, contact your cancer care team as soon as possible. Do not skip or delay treatments without talking to your doctor first, as this could affect how well the medicine works against your cancer.
storage: You do not need to store paclitaxel at home since it is prepared and given to you at the treatment center. If for any reason you are given materials to take home (such as pre-medications), store those as directed on the label, usually at room temperature away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as paclitaxel lowers your ability to fight germs. Avoid live vaccines (such as the flu nasal spray or shingles vaccine) during treatment without asking your doctor first. Do not drink alcohol or take aspirin, ibuprofen, or blood-thinning medicines without checking with your doctor. Avoid pregnancy during treatment, as paclitaxel can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for several months after. Avoid breastfeeding while receiving this medicine. Be careful with sharp objects since paclitaxel can lower your platelet count and make bleeding harder to stop.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bleeding or bruising; severe allergic reaction signs such as difficulty breathing, chest tightness, hives, swelling of the face or throat; severe numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; mouth sores that are very painful or make it hard to eat; extreme tiredness or weakness; shortness of breath or chest pain; or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Do not wait to see if symptoms go away on their own — call right away.
when_it_works: Paclitaxel starts working in your body right away at the cellular level, but it may take several weeks or months of treatment before you or your doctor can see the full effects on your cancer. Your oncology team will monitor your progress through regular blood tests, imaging scans, and check-ups. Everyone responds differently to chemotherapy, so be patient and keep all of your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Paclitaxel can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 2 weeks after your last dose. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as nerve damage, infections, and heart problems. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, your dose may need to be adjusted because your body may not be able to process the medicine properly. Children: Paclitaxel is not commonly used in children, and dosing would be carefully determined by a pediatric oncology specialist. Always tell your entire healthcare team about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as many drugs can interact with paclitaxel.
